notation.meaning: Regressors that vary within units over time
Unit fixed effect: everything permanent about unit $i$
Time fixed effect: shocks common to all units in $t$
Within-unit deviations from the unit's average

blocks.md: Firms, regions and industries differ in countless permanent ways we cannot measure — management quality, location, technology. If those hidden traits are related to both the cause and the outcome, a simple regression mixes them up. Fixed effects solve this by comparing each unit only with itself over time: what happens to a firm's wages when *its own* imports rise? Every permanent trait drops out because it does not change. Adding year effects does the same for shocks that hit every unit in a given year. The price is that only changes within units are used, and anything that changes over time and is correlated with the cause is still a problem.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: It removes a whole class of omitted-variable bias — everything permanent about each unit — at the cost of a single assumption about what does not change.
With unit effects $\alpha_i$ and time effects $\delta_t$:
By the [Frisch-Waugh-Lovell Theorem](note:frisch-waugh-lovell-theorem), including a dummy for each unit gives the same $\hat\beta$ as OLS on demeaned data:

Pooled OLS gives a slope of **−0.08**: firm B has more imports but a much lower outcome level, for reasons unrelated to imports. Within each firm, a 2-unit rise in $x$ comes with a 4-unit rise in $y$, so the fixed-effects slope is **2**. The permanent difference between A and B was driving the pooled result.

sections.heading: What it does and does not fix

blocks.md:
| Problem | Fixed effects |
| --- | --- |
| Permanent unobserved differences across units | Removed by $\alpha_i$ |
| Shocks common to all units in a year | Removed by $\delta_t$ |
| Unobservables that change over time within a unit (e.g. a firm's productivity this year) | **Not** removed — needs an instrument or other design |
| Regressors that never change within a unit | Cannot be estimated (absorbed by $\alpha_i$) |
| Measurement error in $x$ | Often made worse: within-unit variation is smaller, so noise is a larger share ([Classical Measurement Error](note:classical-measurement-error)) |

- Believing fixed effects make a regression causal. Time-varying confounders remain: highly productive firm-years both trade more and pay more.
- Including a time-invariant regressor and expecting a coefficient for it.
- Forgetting that standard errors should usually be clustered by unit, since errors for the same unit are correlated over time ([Clustered Standard Errors](note:clustered-standard-errors)).

- Panel data everywhere: firms over time, regions over time, workers over time.
- The backbone of [Difference-in-Differences](note:difference-in-differences) with unit and time effects.
